questions.stem: In New Kingdom ideology, a central duty of the king as god-king was to:
options: uphold maat, the divine order, against the forces of chaos
lead the daily rituals in every temple of Egypt in person
choose the High Priest of each god by public election
share the rule of Egypt equally with the High Priest of Amun
questions.explanation: The king was the son of Ra and the living Horus, and his role was to maintain maat (order, truth and justice) against isfet (chaos), in war and in the temples. In practice priests performed the daily rituals on his behalf, and the High Priest of Amun was appointed by the king rather than ruling beside him.

questions.stem: Scenes of the king smiting foreign enemies were carved on the pylons of temples such as Karnak mainly to:
options: warn priests that the king could punish them for disloyalty
mark the entrance through which foreign envoys entered the temple
show the king defending Egypt and the gods' order against chaos
record the exact numbers of prisoners taken in a single campaign
questions.explanation: The smiting scene was a standard image of royal power: the king crushing foreigners stood for order defeating chaos, whatever the actual campaign. It was ideological rather than a precise record, so it cannot be read for exact prisoner numbers.

questions.stem: In the New Kingdom, the title God's Wife of Amun was:
options: an honour granted to the widow of each High Priest of Amun
a priestly office held by royal women, with its own estates and income
a title given to the foreign princesses married to the king for diplomatic ties
the name for the priestesses of Hathor at the workers' village
questions.explanation: The God's Wife of Amun was a powerful priestly office held by royal women, beginning with Ahmose-Nefertari, and it came with estates and staff. Hatshepsut held the title before she became king, which gave her a religious and economic base at Thebes.

questions.stem: The highest-ranking priest in the cult of Amun at Karnak held the title:
options: Overseer of the Granaries
Scribe of the Tomb
First Prophet of Amun
King's Son of Kush
questions.explanation: The High Priest of Amun was called the First Prophet (hem-netjer tepy) of Amun. The King's Son of Kush governed Nubia, the Overseer of the Granaries ran grain stores, and the Scribe of the Tomb kept records for the Deir el-Medineh crew.

questions.stem: Under kings such as Thutmosis III, a large share of the booty and tribute from foreign campaigns was given to the temple of Amun at Karnak. Over time, one consequence was:
options: the Amun priesthood became a wealthy and powerful institution
the king lost the right to appoint the High Priest of Amun
the god Amun was replaced by Ptah as the state's chief god
the temple of Karnak was closed to all priests but the king
questions.explanation: Kings thanked Amun for victory with land, gold, captives and goods, so Karnak became the richest temple in Egypt and its priesthood a major economic and political force. Kings still appointed the High Priest, and Amun-Ra remained the chief state god apart from the Amarna interlude.

questions.stem: A document from Deir el-Medineh records that a woman named Naunakhte made a will disinheriting several of her children who had not cared for her in old age. This source best supports the view that New Kingdom women could:
options: inherit property only through a husband who had died
make a will only with a male guardian's written consent
hold the offices of vizier and scribe if they were widowed
own property and decide for themselves who inherited it
questions.explanation: Naunakhte acted in her own name, which fits wider evidence that Egyptian women could own, buy, sell and bequeath property and take part in legal cases. Nothing in the will required a guardian's consent, and women did not hold the vizierate.

questions.stem: Texts copied in scribal schools urge pupils to ‘be a scribe’ and describe the farmer, soldier and craftsman as miserable and overworked. A historian using these texts as evidence of other occupations should note that:
options: they were written to make pupils value the scribe's career, so they exaggerate
they were written by farmers and soldiers to complain about their own harsh work
they were royal decrees that fixed the duties of each occupation by law
they describe Old Kingdom conditions that had vanished by the New Kingdom
questions.explanation: These school texts were written by scribes for trainee scribes, and their purpose was to promote the scribal career by contrast, so their picture of other trades is deliberately bleak. They are useful for scribal attitudes but must be corroborated, for example with tomb scenes and ostraca, before they are used for the lives of farmers or soldiers.

questions.stem: Scribes held a privileged place in New Kingdom society mainly because:
options: they were exempt from serving the king or the temples in any way
they were all priests who served in the temple of Amun at Karnak
literacy was rare and the state relied on them to keep its records
only the sons of kings were permitted to learn to read and write
questions.explanation: Only a small minority could read and write, and the administration of taxes, grain, temples, the army and the tombs depended on scribes. They served the state and the temples rather than being exempt, and most were not royal sons or priests.

questions.stem: In tomb paintings such as those of Menna, a scribe of the fields, officials measure the crops with ropes and farmers who have not paid are beaten. These scenes show that agricultural workers:
options: were assessed for tax on their harvest and punished if they failed to pay
owned their own land outright and paid nothing at all to the state or the temples
were paid in silver coins for the grain they delivered to the granaries
worked only during the inundation, when the fields were under water
questions.explanation: Officials measured fields and estimated the harvest so a share could be taken as tax in grain, and tomb scenes show defaulters being punished. Egypt had no coinage in this period, and farm work happened after the flood receded, not while the fields were under water.

questions.stem: The men of the workers' village of Deir el-Medineh were employed mainly to:
options: cut and decorate the royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings
build and repair the pylons of the temple of Karnak
farm the estates of Amun on the west bank at Thebes
quarry granite at Aswan for the obelisks of the kings at Karnak
questions.explanation: Deir el-Medineh housed the specialist crew of stonecutters, plasterers, draughtsmen and painters who made the royal tombs. Temple building, farming and quarrying were done by other workforces.

questions.stem: The Deir el-Medineh crew was organised as:
options: two ‘sides’, each with a foreman, and a scribe who recorded the work
a gang of slaves owned by the vizier and guarded day and night by Medjay troops
a temple guild run by the High Priest of Amun from Karnak
independent craftsmen who bid against each other for each tomb
questions.explanation: The crew was divided into a left and a right side, each led by a foreman and deputy, while the Scribe of the Tomb recorded work, absences and rations. The workers were free, state-employed craftsmen answerable through the vizier; the Medjay policed the necropolis but did not own or guard the crew as slaves.

questions.stem: Thousands of ostraca survive from Deir el-Medineh. They are especially valuable to historians because they:
options: are clay tablets of letters exchanged with Near Eastern kings
record everyday matters such as absences, sales and disputes
were carved by royal order to celebrate the king's victories
are papyrus copies of temple rituals made for the priests
questions.explanation: Ostraca are flakes of limestone and broken pottery used for everyday notes, so they give a rare view of ordinary life, including work registers that list reasons for absence. They were not royal monuments, temple papyri or cuneiform tablets.

questions.stem: Ostraca from Deir el-Medineh record goods such as a coffin being valued in deben and then paid for with grain, oil and cloth. This shows that the village economy:
options: used the deben of copper as a measure of value while goods were bartered
used silver coins stamped with the king's name to pay for most goods
had prices fixed by the vizier for every item sold in the village
required every purchase to be paid in copper bars of a set weight
questions.explanation: The deben was a weight of copper used as a unit of account: goods were valued in deben but usually exchanged for other goods of equal value. Coinage did not reach Egypt until much later, and the ostraca show prices being negotiated between individuals rather than fixed by the state.

questions.stem: In Year 29 of Rameses III, the Deir el-Medineh workers stopped work and sat behind the temples on the west bank. According to the Turin Strike Papyrus, the main cause was:
options: the vizier had ordered them to work on the king's palace
Libyan raiders had attacked and burned their village
the priests had refused to let them worship Amun
their grain rations had not been delivered on time
questions.explanation: The papyrus, written by the scribe Amennakht, records the men protesting that they were hungry because their rations were overdue. It is often called the earliest recorded strike, and it points to strains in the state's ability to supply its own workforce.

questions.stem: Late in the 20th Dynasty, papyri record trials of men who robbed royal and noble tombs, and accusations that some Theban officials protected the robbers. Taken together with the Year 29 strike, these sources suggest:
options: a revolt by the Amun priesthood that deposed the reigning king
that the Sea Peoples had occupied Thebes and looted its temples
economic strain and weakening royal authority in the Theban region
that the court had moved to Nubia and abandoned the royal tombs
questions.explanation: Late payments to the tomb workers and widespread tomb robbery both point to shortages and to a state that could no longer reliably protect its necropolis or pay its servants. The trial records show local robbers acting for gain while the court stayed in Egypt, and the Sea Peoples never reached Thebes.

questions.stem: Shabti figures were placed in New Kingdom tombs in order to:
options: record the dead person's titles for visitors to the tomb chapel
do the work the dead person might be called on to do in the afterlife
stand guard at the entrance to the tomb against robbers and wild animals
hold the organs that had been removed during mummification
questions.explanation: Shabtis were small figures inscribed with a spell so they would answer when the deceased was summoned to labour in the fields of the afterlife. Organs went into canopic jars, and titles were recorded on the walls and stelae of the tomb chapel.

questions.stem: In the judgement scene of the Book of the Dead, the heart of the dead person is weighed against:
options: the crook and flail
the eye of Horus
the ka of the king
the feather of Maat
questions.explanation: The heart was weighed against the feather of Maat, goddess of truth and order; a heart heavy with wrongdoing was devoured by Ammit. The crook and flail were royal regalia, not part of the weighing.

questions.stem: New Kingdom kings were buried in hidden rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings, while their mortuary temples stood apart on the edge of the cultivation. The main reason for this separation was to:
options: move the royal cult away from Thebes to the new capital in the Delta
keep the burial secure while the offering cult continued in public
obey a law of the priests of Ptah that banned burial near temples
allow the tomb and temple to share a single entrance passage
questions.explanation: Pyramids had marked royal burials and attracted robbers, so New Kingdom kings hid their tombs in the valley and placed the temple where offerings were made to the dead king in plain view. The temples were on the Theban west bank, so the cult did not move to the Delta.

questions.stem: The tomb of Seti I in the Valley of the Kings is notable for:
options: being found intact with its treasure by Howard Carter in 1922
its stone pyramid built above the burial chamber on the hillside
its painted reliefs of Seti's son Rameses II winning the Battle of Kadesh
its length and its decoration with funerary texts such as the Book of Gates
questions.explanation: Seti I's tomb, opened by Giovanni Belzoni in 1817, is one of the longest and most completely decorated in the valley, with texts such as the Book of Gates and the Amduat guiding the king through the underworld. The intact tomb found in 1922 was Tutankhamun's.

questions.stem: The tomb of the Vizier Rekhmire at Thebes is especially valuable to historians because its paintings and texts include:
options: the duties of the vizier and scenes of foreign tribute and workshops
the only surviving Egyptian account of the Battle of Kadesh
the official records of the strike by the tomb workers under Rameses III
a list of every king of Egypt from Narmer to Thutmosis III
questions.explanation: Rekhmire served Thutmosis III, and his tomb records the Duties of the Vizier and shows delegations from Punt, Nubia, Syria and the Aegean bringing goods, as well as craftsmen at work. Kadesh came under Rameses II, and the strike under Rameses III, long after his time.

questions.stem: A historian uses noble tombs such as Rekhmire's as evidence of daily life in Thebes. The most important limitation of this evidence is that the scenes:
options: show only the king, so they reveal nothing about officials or workers
present an idealised, ordered world intended to serve the owner in eternity
were painted centuries later by priests who had never seen the tomb's owner
were copied directly from Mesopotamian models and show foreign customs
questions.explanation: Tomb scenes were made for the owner's afterlife and self-presentation, so they show a prosperous, orderly world and the owner at his best, leaving out failure and hardship. They do show officials and workers in detail and were made in the owner's own time, so the problem is their purpose, not their date or subject.

questions.stem: The Great Hypostyle Hall of the temple of Karnak was built and decorated mainly under:
options: Hatshepsut and Thutmosis III
Rameses III and Rameses IX
Ahmose and Amenhotep I
Seti I and Rameses II
questions.explanation: The hall, with its 134 columns, was decorated chiefly under Seti I and completed by his son Rameses II. Hatshepsut and Thutmosis III built elsewhere at Karnak, including obelisks and the Akh-menu.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a ruler and a building project is correct?
options: Thutmosis III – the Ramesseum on the west bank
Hatshepsut – the mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri
Rameses III – the temples at Abu Simbel in Nubia
Rameses II – the mortuary temple of Medinet Habu
questions.explanation: Hatshepsut's terraced temple, Djeser-djeseru, stands at Deir el-Bahri. Abu Simbel and the Ramesseum belong to Rameses II, and Medinet Habu is the mortuary temple of Rameses III.

questions.stem: A statue in the style of an earlier king carries the cartouches of Rameses II, carved over an older, partly erased name. The most likely explanation is that:
options: the statue was a gift to Rameses II from the Hittite king
Rameses II re-inscribed an earlier king's statue as his own
the earlier king had copied a statue made for Rameses II
Rameses II's priests carved the statue for his coronation
questions.explanation: Rameses II often usurped older monuments by recutting their inscriptions, a quick way to fill Egypt with his name and image. A statue in an earlier style with an erased name cannot have been made for Rameses first, so recutting is the best reading.

questions.stem: Rameses II built the great temple at Abu Simbel, with four colossal statues of himself, in Nubia. Its location suggests it was intended to:
options: assert the king's divine power over Nubia and those entering Egypt
serve as the king's burial place, far from the robbers of Thebes
honour the Hittite king after the peace treaty between them
provide a new capital for Egypt close to the gold mines
questions.explanation: Abu Simbel's colossi faced travellers on the Nile coming north from Nubia, proclaiming Egyptian royal and divine power in conquered territory. Rameses II was buried in the Valley of the Kings and moved his residence to Pi-Rameses in the Delta, not to Nubia.

questions.stem: In the New Kingdom, the civil administration of Egypt was headed by:
options: two viziers, one for Upper Egypt and one for Lower Egypt
a council of nomarchs elected by each of the provinces
the High Priest of Amun, who governed for the king
the King's Son of Kush, who ruled from the Delta
questions.explanation: By the reign of Thutmosis III the vizierate was divided between a southern vizier at Thebes and a northern one at Memphis, both answering to the king. The King's Son of Kush governed Nubia, and nomarchs were appointed officials, not elected.

questions.stem: Nubia was valuable to New Kingdom Egypt above all as a source of:
options: horses and chariots for the royal army
gold, as well as ivory, ebony and soldiers
cedar timber for ships and temple doors
lapis lazuli for royal and temple jewellery
questions.explanation: Nubian gold underpinned Egyptian wealth and diplomacy, and Nubia also supplied ivory, ebony, cattle and troops. Cedar came from Lebanon, lapis lazuli from distant Afghanistan through trade, and horses from the Near East.

questions.stem: At the Battle of Kadesh, Rameses II's army marched in four divisions named after:
options: the gods Amun, Ra, Ptah and Seth
the four sons of Horus who guarded the organs
the four provinces of Upper and Lower Egypt
the kings Ahmose, Thutmosis, Amenhotep and Seti
questions.explanation: The Egyptian accounts name the divisions of Amun, Ra (Pre), Ptah and Seth, each made up of chariotry and infantry. Naming them after gods tied the army to the state religion and the king's role as the gods' champion.

questions.stem: Reliefs of Rameses II's army show Sherden warriors in horned helmets fighting for Egypt. This suggests that the New Kingdom army:
options: included foreign troops, some of them former enemies, as soldiers
was made up only of Egyptian conscripts from the farming villages
was commanded by Sherden generals after Rameses II's accession
fought only at sea, where the Sherden were the main sailors
questions.explanation: The Sherden appear earlier as raiders, but Rameses II recruited them, including as part of his guard. The New Kingdom army was a professional force that included foreign units; Egyptians still held command, and it fought chiefly on land.

questions.stem: Hatshepsut's expedition to Punt, shown in reliefs at Deir el-Bahri, brought back goods such as:
options: horses and bronze weapons from the Hittites
myrrh trees, incense, ebony and exotic animals
cedar logs, olive oil and Cretan pottery
copper ingots and tin from the mines of Cyprus
questions.explanation: The reliefs show ships loaded with living incense trees, myrrh, ebony, ivory, gold and animals such as baboons, from Punt, a land probably on the African coast of the Red Sea. The other goods came from Lebanon, the Aegean, Cyprus and Anatolia, not Punt.

questions.stem: Thutmosis III's Annals list goods from the king of Assyria as inu, a word usually translated as ‘tribute’. Historians are cautious about this because:
options: the Annals were written by Assyrian scribes who disliked the Egyptians
the word inu referred only to grain taxes collected inside Egypt itself
royal texts presented gifts from independent powers as tribute to honour the king
Assyria was in fact a province of Egypt, governed by an Egyptian viceroy from Assur
questions.explanation: Egyptian royal ideology placed all foreign lands beneath the king, so even gifts from distant, independent rulers were labelled as tribute. Assyria was never an Egyptian province, so the label tells us about Egyptian ideology more than about actual subjection.

questions.stem: Papyrus Harris I records the vast estates, workers and goods that Rameses III gave to the temples, above all to Amun at Thebes. A historian is most likely to use this source to argue that:
options: Egypt's trade with Punt ended because of Rameses III's gifts
royal gifts strengthened the Amun priesthood relative to the crown
Rameses III closed the temples to pay for his long wars with the Libyans
the temples paid the king's army in the Sea Peoples' wars
questions.explanation: The scale of the donations, especially to Amun, shows how much of Egypt's land and labour had passed to the temples, which helps explain the growing power of the High Priests of Amun in the late 20th Dynasty. The papyrus records giving to the temples, not closing them, and it also mentions an expedition to Punt.

questions.stem: According to the Annals of Thutmosis III at Karnak, before the Battle of Megiddo the king:
options: waited for Hittite troops to join him before advancing
chose the narrow Aruna pass against the advice of his officers
made a treaty with the prince of Kadesh to avoid a battle
sent his army by sea to land behind the city of Megiddo
questions.explanation: The Annals describe the officers urging one of the safer, wider roads while the king insisted on the direct Aruna pass, which surprised the enemy coalition led by the prince of Kadesh. The story also served to show the king's courage and divine guidance.

questions.stem: After the Egyptian victory outside Megiddo, the Annals say the city was not taken at once because:
options: his soldiers stopped to loot the enemy camp, letting the enemy escape inside
a Hittite relief army arrived and forced Thutmosis III to retreat south to Gaza
the king's officers refused to attack a city sacred to the god Baal
a flood of the Kishon river cut the Egyptian army off from the city
questions.explanation: The Annals admit that the troops turned to looting the camp, letting the defeated princes be hauled up into the city, which then had to be besieged for about seven months. This rare admission of a mistake is one reason the account is thought to draw on army records.

questions.stem: The Annals of Thutmosis III were carved on the walls of the temple of Amun at Karnak. A historian evaluating them as evidence should consider that they:
options: honoured Amun and the king, so they stress success and pass over setbacks
were written by the defeated princes of Syria and so minimise Egypt's role
were composed under Rameses II, two centuries after the events they describe
were private letters never intended for anyone but the king's family to read
questions.explanation: The Annals drew on campaign records but were displayed in Amun's temple as thanks for victory, so their purpose was to glorify the god and the king. That purpose shapes what they include, though they were composed in Thutmosis III's own reign.

questions.stem: Thutmosis III took the sons of defeated Syrian rulers to Egypt to be raised at court and later sent them home to rule. The main purpose of this policy was to:
options: hold hostages and create loyal, Egyptianised vassal rulers
train them as priests to spread the cult of Amun in Syria
give them as slaves to the temples of Amun and Ptah
prepare them to command the Egyptian army against Mitanni
questions.explanation: The princes guaranteed their fathers' loyalty while in Egypt and, raised at court, were expected to rule as loyal vassals when they returned. The aim was control of Syria-Palestine, not converting it or enslaving its royal families.

questions.stem: At the Battle of Kadesh in 1274 BCE, the Egyptian army was caught by surprise mainly because:
options: the Hittite king had signed a truce with Rameses and then broken it overnight
Rameses II had sent his chariotry home before the battle began
the division of Amun deserted to the Hittites before the battle
captured Shasu spies falsely said the Hittite army was far to the north
questions.explanation: Two Shasu told Rameses II that the Hittites were near Aleppo, so he pushed ahead with the division of Amun; the Hittite chariotry then struck the division of Ra on the march and attacked the camp. There had been no truce, and the divisions were strung out rather than deserting.

questions.stem: Rameses II's accounts of Kadesh on temple walls describe a great victory won by the king almost alone. Historians generally judge the battle a stalemate because:
options: the Hittite king surrendered Kadesh and then took it back
no Egyptian source mentions the battle after his reign
Kadesh stayed in Hittite hands and Hittite records claim success
Rameses II's own temple accounts openly admit that he lost the battle
questions.explanation: Despite the Egyptian claims, Rameses II withdrew without taking Kadesh, and Hittite texts show the Hittites advancing afterwards into territory south of Kadesh. The Egyptian accounts celebrate the king's personal bravery and never admit defeat, so outside sources are needed to weigh them.

questions.stem: The treaty made by Rameses II and the Hittite king Khattushili III, about 16 years after Kadesh, included terms on:
options: Egypt's annexation of Hatti and the Hittite payment of tribute
the transfer of the city of Kadesh to permanent Egyptian rule
the conversion of the Hittites to the worship of Amun-Ra
non-aggression, mutual defence and the return of fugitives
questions.explanation: The treaty bound both kings not to attack each other, to help each other against attack and rebellion, and to return fugitives, who were to be treated humanely. It recognised the two kingdoms as equals rather than giving Kadesh or tribute to Egypt.

questions.stem: The treaty between Rameses II and Khattushili III survives in an Egyptian hieroglyphic version at Karnak and a cuneiform version from the Hittite capital. The existence of both versions allows historians to:
options: show that the treaty was never ratified by the Hittite king
compare them and see how each side presented itself to its own people
prove that Egypt dictated every term to a defeated Hittite kingdom
date the Battle of Kadesh to the very day it was fought
questions.explanation: Comparing the two versions shows a shared core of terms, while each side's version frames the other king as having asked for peace. That corroboration is a strength, and the differences reveal each court's propaganda rather than showing one side dictating to a defeated enemy.

questions.stem: Merenptah's stele recording his victory over the Libyans is especially famous because it:
options: lists the Hittite cities that fell to Egypt after Kadesh
is widely seen as the earliest mention of Israel outside the Bible
records the first treaty Egypt made with the Sea Peoples
describes the burial of his father Rameses II in the Valley of the Kings
questions.explanation: The stele, from Merenptah's fifth year, celebrates his defeat of a Libyan invasion and adds a list of subdued places in Canaan that includes a people called Israel. It records victory over the Libyans and their allies, not a treaty with the Sea Peoples.

questions.stem: In Year 8 of Rameses III, Egypt defeated a coalition of Sea Peoples, including the Peleset, in battles on land and in the Delta. The main source for these battles is:
options: the Amarna Letters sent by the vassal kings of Canaan
the painted tomb of the Vizier Rekhmire at Sheikh Abd el-Qurna
the Annals of Thutmosis III in the temple of Karnak
the reliefs and texts of his mortuary temple at Medinet Habu
questions.explanation: Medinet Habu shows the naval battle in the Delta and the land battle, with the Sea Peoples' distinctive headdresses and ships. The Amarna Letters, Rekhmire's tomb and Thutmosis III's Annals all come from the 18th Dynasty, long before Rameses III.

questions.stem: Rameses III fought Libyan invaders in his fifth and eleventh years and the Sea Peoples in his eighth. What do these wars suggest about Egypt in the 20th Dynasty?
options: Egypt was allied with the Libyans against the Hittite kingdom
Egypt's army had been disbanded and replaced by temple guards
Egypt was now defending its own borders against migrating peoples
Egypt was expanding its empire to the Euphrates for the first time
questions.explanation: Under Thutmosis III Egypt campaigned far into Syria, but Rameses III fought on Egypt's own frontiers against Libyans and Sea Peoples seeking land. Egypt survived, but its Near Eastern empire was soon lost and the state weakened.

questions.stem: Which development best explains the weakening of royal authority in Thebes by the end of the 20th Dynasty in 1069 BCE?
options: the growing wealth of the Amun priesthood and economic strain on the state
the Hyksos reconquest of the Delta and the closing of the trade routes
Akhenaten's closing of the temples of Amun and the loss of all their income
a Hittite invasion that captured Memphis and the northern vizierate
questions.explanation: The late 20th Dynasty saw grain shortages, unpaid workers, tomb robbery and the loss of the Near Eastern empire, while the High Priests of Amun gained great wealth and eventually control of Thebes. Akhenaten's reign and the Hyksos lay centuries earlier, and the Hittite kingdom had itself collapsed.
